html:
The Battle of Ayacucho was fought on 9 December 1824 on a high plain near Ayacucho in the Andes of southern Peru. A patriot army under Antonio José de Sucre beat the last large Spanish army in South America.

Peru was Spain's strongest base on the continent. José de San Martín had declared its independence in 1821, but royalist troops still held the highlands. Simón Bolívar arrived in 1823, won at Junín in August 1824 and left Sucre in command. Sucre had about 5,800 men from Gran Colombia, Peru and beyond. The viceroy, José de la Serna, had more men and more guns, and held the heights above the plain. When the royalists came down to attack, Sucre struck before they had formed their lines. The viceroy was wounded and captured, and the battle was over in about two hours.

That evening the royalists signed a surrender that covered all Spanish forces in Peru. It ended the Spanish American independence wars on the mainland, apart from a few forts. The next year Upper Peru became the new state of Bolivia, named after Bolívar, with Sucre as one of its first presidents.
